title: When Something Goes Wrong
topic: complaining and solving a problem politely
why: Last lesson of the travel unit: when something goes wrong, the learner can report a problem, politely ask for a solution with the phrase ¿Podría…?, and say they've forgotten or lost something (se me ha olvidado). They also learn to make themselves understood at the doctor's and the pharmacy, reusing the perfecto, usted and the imperative from the previous lesson.

{"lessons": ["

Reporting a problem politely

Broken air conditioning, a mistake on the bill, a room that hasn't been cleaned: when you travel, you need to know how to complain without being rude. In Spain, people stay direct but courteous, and they almost always start with Perdone.

To say…In Spanish
it doesn't workNo funciona el aire acondicionado. / La ducha no funciona.
there's a problem with…Hay un problema con la factura.
there's no…No hay agua caliente. / No hay toallas.
it's dirtyLa habitación está sucia.
there's a lot of noiseHay mucho ruido en la calle.
I'd like to make a complaintQuería hacer una reclamación.

Asking for a solution: ¿Podría…?

¿Podría…? (could you…?) is the most polite way to ask for something. It's a conditional, a tense you'll study later: for now, just learn it as a set phrase, followed by an infinitive, exactly like English \"could you + verb\".

¿Podría llamar a un técnico, por favor?Could you call a technician, please?
¿Podría cambiar las toallas?Could you change the towels?

What the staff will say

Lo siento mucho (I'm very sorry), Perdone las molestias (sorry for the inconvenience), Ahora mismo (right away), No se preocupe (don't worry, a negative form you just need to recognize).

In Spain, every business must have a hoja de reclamaciones, an official complaint form. Just asking for it often solves the problem! Watch out: the word reclamación means \"complaint,\" not \"reclamation.\"

", "

Se me ha olvidado, se me ha perdido

To say you forgot or lost something by accident, Spanish speakers use a very common construction. Take it as a set expression: se me ha olvidado (I forgot), se me ha perdido (I lost), se me ha roto (I broke).

Se me ha olvidado el pasaporte en el hotel.I left my passport at the hotel.

Word for word: \"the passport has gotten forgotten on me.\" That's why the verb agrees with the thing forgotten, not with the person:

One thingSeveral things
Se me ha olvidado la llave.Se me han olvidado las llaves.
Se me ha perdido el móvil.Se me han perdido las gafas.
Se me ha roto el vaso.Se me han roto los vasos.

For someone else, you only change me: ¿Se te ha olvidado algo? (did you forget something?), se nos ha perdido el perro (we've lost the dog).

You can also say He olvidado el pasaporte or He perdido las llaves: that's correct, but more neutral. Se me ha olvidado stresses that it wasn't your fault, it just happened, a bit like English \"the glass broke\" instead of \"I broke the glass\"!

", "

At the doctor's and the pharmacy

To say where it hurts, Spanish uses doler, which works like gustar: the body part is the subject (\"my head hurts,\" not \"I hurt my head\"). So me duele for one thing, me duelen for several.

SymptomIn Spanish
I have a headacheMe duele la cabeza.
my feet hurtMe duelen los pies.
I have a sore throatMe duele la garganta.
I have a feverTengo fiebre.
I have a coughTengo tos.
I have a cold (man / woman)Estoy resfriado / resfriada. (or constipado / constipada)
I feel dizzyEstoy mareado / mareada.

Remember the false friend: constipado means \"having a cold,\" not \"constipated\"!

The doctor's advice

The doctor addresses the patient formally and gives advice in the usted imperative you've just learned:

Abra la boca. Tome una pastilla cada ocho horas, beba mucha agua y descanse.Open your mouth. Take a pill every eight hours, drink lots of water and get some rest.

At the pharmacy

Buenos días. ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de garganta? — Sí, tenemos un jarabe muy bueno: tome una cucharada dos veces al día.Good morning. Do you have anything for a sore throat? — Yes, we have a very good syrup: take one spoonful twice a day.

In Spain, pharmacies have a glowing green cross, and at night there's always a farmacia de guardia (on-duty pharmacy). False friend alert: la receta means \"the prescription\" (and also a cooking \"recipe\"), never a \"receipt.\"
